catalog_locator: ch. 5 Conclusions, p. 67; sec. 4.1 Reduced syllables, p. 53; sec. 4.2 head, p. 54; sec. 4.2.2.2 Word-final syllables, pp. 63-64; sec. 1.3 Language contact and the Amdo Sprachbund, p. 7; Kerbs 2021 sec. 4.4.4, p. 24
catalog_quote: p. 67: "Another non-Sinitic trait is the reduced tonality of Gangou compared to Mandarin varieties in other parts of China. Additional research is needed to determine the exact nature of the Gangou tone system, but it is clear that it shows similarities with other Amdo Sinitic varieties: it consists of maximally three tones (possibly only two, if the contrast between the low tone and the rising tone turns out to be allophonic), and there is extensive tone neutralization in non-initial syllables. Stress (and possible ensuing tonal reduction) may play an important role in the prosodic system of Gangou." p. 53: "Gangou syllables can be divided into monomoraic and bimoraic syllables. The majority of Gangou syllables belong to the latter group. The former group consists of syllables of the type described above for Standard Mandarin, i.e. syllable-final, destressed syllables, and of syllables containing one of the vowels i or u, which can appear anywhere inside a word. ... When stressed or occurring in monosyllables, they are usually fully lengthened." p. 64: "The reason for the variation among non-C syllables is not clear at the present moment and more research is needed to determine whether the contrast is allotonic or whether it is due to other factors, such as stress or tone deletion."

new_statements.citation: Kerbs, Richard. 2019. The Phonology of Gangou: A Chinese Variety of the Amdo Sprachbund. MA thesis, University of Helsinki.
new_statements.locator: ch. 5 Conclusions, p. 67 (with sec. 4.2 p. 54 and sec. 4.1 p. 53)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (77 pp., text present, author metadata 'Richard Kerbs', Word 2019). The p. 67 quote is on PDF page 72 (printed p. 67, ch. 5 Conclusions) and matches verbatim: 'Another non-Sinitic trait is the reduced tonality of Gangou.. it consists of maximally three tones (possibly only two, if the contrast between the low tone and the rising tone turns out to be allophonic), and there is extensive tone neutralization in non-initial syllables. Stress (and possible ensuing tonal reduction) may play an important role in the prosodic system of Gangou.' The p. 54 quote ('It is shown that Gangou has three tones underlyingly, which are reduced to two in monosyllables.') is verbatim at the head of sec. 4…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gangou is a (reduced) tone language: three lexical tones /11, 35, 55/ contrast on the first syllable of di-/polysyllables, only two (high vs low-rising) on isolation monosyllables; non-initial syllables show extensive tone neutralization and there are 'reduced/destressed' monomoraic syllables (SM-neutral-tone type word-finally, plus reduced i/u syllables in any position). The source gives NO rule for where word stress falls; it explicitly flags stress as an open question that 'may play an important role'. Kerbs 2021 (Himalayan Linguistics 20(3): 12, 23-24) restates the 2-3-tone analysis and never mentions stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Toneless enclitics (e.g. perfect -lio) take their pitch from the preceding syllable; possible Hui vs non-Hui differences untested; author unsure whether low vs rising contrast is phonemic.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone analysis restricted to monosyllables (isolation/utterance-final) and disyllabic words; the full tonal contrast is word-initial, suggesting a left-headed tonal domain (Kerbs 2021: 24 compares Shanghai), but this is not framed as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kerbs's data: three speakers (one Tu/Monguor woman, two Han men) from Gangou Township, Minhe County, recorded 2017 in Gangou and Xining; Hui speakers' Gangou not sampled and may differ. Same variety as Glottolog gang1272 'Gangou' (no ISO code); locally part of the Ledu–Minhe group of Qinghai (Zhongyuan/Northwest) Mandarin, heavily restructured under Mangghuer (Minhe Monguor) contact.

tone_statements.citation: Kerbs, Richard. 2021. The phonology of Gangou from a comparative perspective. Himalayan Linguistics 20(3): 8-27. doi:10.5070/H920353989
tone_statements.quote: Gān’gōu also has two to three tones, depending on the syllable type. [p. 11] ... What seems to be clear is that, in monosyllabic words uttered in isolation, there are two tones, a high tone and a low-rising tone. ... Three tones have been observed, at least on the phonetic level: a high, a rising, and a low tone. This is based on the observation of tones of the first syllable of disyllabic words. ... The particle -lio, on the other hand, appears to be a toneless syllable, because its phonetic realization—which can be either low-rising, high or low, as evident from the examples in (23)—depends on the tone of the preceding syllable. [p. 23] ... It is not clear at present, however, whether this three-way contrast is phonemic or whether the tonal system of Gān’gōu could be reduced to a two-tone system. [p. 24]
tone_statements.locator: sec. 3, p. 11; sec. 4.4.4 Tone Reduction, pp. 23-24
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: The article finds two tones (high, low-rising) on isolated monosyllables, three (high, rising, low) on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and a toneless perfect particle -lio whose pitch follows the preceding syllable, and it leaves open whether the three-way contrast is phonemic. It never mentions word stress; the catalog entry already lists this article as its supporting source and its lexi

sources.locator: ch. 5 Conclusions, p. 67 (with sec. 4.2 p. 54 and sec. 4.1 p. 53)
sources.note: Only dedicated phonology of Gangou. Ch. 4 'Suprasegmental phonology' (pp. 53-66): Gangou is tonal -- three underlying tones (11, 35, 55), reduced to two in monosyllables, extensive tone neutralization in non-initial syllables; 4.1 describes 'reduced (destressed, monomoraic) syllables', more frequent than Standard Mandarin neutral tone and not confined to word-final position. No rule for word-stress placement; p. 67 explicitly: 'Stress (and possible ensuing tonal reduction) may play an important role in the prosodic system of Gangou' -- i.e. stress left uninvestigated.

sources.citation: Kerbs, Richard. 2021. The sound system of Gangou from a comparative perspective. Himalayan Linguistics 20(3): 8-27. doi:10.5070/H920353989.
sources.note: Sec. 3 (p. 12): 'Gān'gōu also has two to three tones, depending on the syllable type'; sec. 4.4.4 Tone reduction (pp. 23-24): two tones on isolation monosyllables (high vs low-rising), three on first syllables of disyllables, toneless enclitic -lio; first syllable of a tonal domain is tone-bearing. The word 'stress' does not occur; no stress statement.
